channel.title: With-Deepseek-V4-Pro
channel.description: Technical notes by Jaehun Ryu, a deep learning compiler engineer, on LLM inference, KV caches, compilers, C++, AI papers, and open-source code.

item.title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

Agent-based services do not end with a single request. Because they wait on tools, summarize context, and spin up sub-tasks in parallel, the same prefix ends up being recomputed multiple times. Evolving Infra reduces this repeated computation by adjusting node role assignments in real time to match the agent workload composition, and KV eviction and routing to match the agent’s context management signals.

item.title: RidgeFill: Training-Free Late-Layer Cache Fill for Faster Prefill
item.description:
Paper

Introduction: The wait before an answer appears

With a long prompt, the model must pass the entire document through before the first token emerges, and the user waits the whole time seeing nothing. To cut that wait, RidgeFill skips computation in some layers and prefills the cache those layers would have produced by approximating it. No training is needed, and the tail, some selected rows, and every decoding step are computed exactly.

item.title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents
item.description:
Paper

Long tool observations make agents slow and blur their judgment

The longer tool observations get, the more the context costs to compute and the more judgment wavers. This paper proposes compressing tool results not into text but into continuous vectors, keeping only the information the agent needs to decide its next action. The code is released at https://github.com/THU-Agent/Coca-cola .

item.title: AutoCompress: Automated Hardware-Guided Model Compression
item.description:
Paper

AutoCompress: Model Compression That Puts Serving Constraints Directly into the Search Objective

Introduction

When engineers deploy a large language model to a real service, the first question they hit is not “how much should we shrink it?” but “which axis should we shrink, and by how much, to survive on this device and this workload?” AutoCompress (NVIDIA, arXiv:2611.08290) turns that question into a cost model measured directly in the serving engine, and finds the answer by putting latency, throughput, and memory limits into the architecture search objective. This post starts from the problem that “parameter count alone cannot predict serving cost,” then covers examples of what remains and what disappears when one axis is narrowed, each step of the method, and results from three deployment scenarios and the 120B single-GPU case, in that order.

item.title: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

A looped transformer is a model that reuses the same group of layers several times. It saves parameters, but each iteration step has to keep its own key/value cache, so the serving bottleneck shifts from the weights to the cache. This post summarizes the observations, design, and measured results of LoopVQ, a method that compresses that cache to under 1 bit per element.

item.title: FLAMIA: FLAsh MIcroscaling Attention for Fast and Causally Safe Training on Blackwell
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

Blackwell GPUs execute FP8 and FP4 matrix multiplies 2x and 4x faster than BF16, respectively. To bring that speed to attention, the first problem to solve is not precision loss but whether “a quantized value is reconstructed identically in the forward and backward computations.” FLAMIA designs this condition inside a low-bit attention kernel and turns it into training calls that are actually faster on Blackwell.

item.title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding
item.description:
Paper

SpecOPD: Training Speculative Decoding Drafters with Branch Parallelism

Introduction

Speculative decoding speeds up generation by having a small drafter propose multiple tokens that a large target verifies in a single pass. But the ceiling on that speed is set by how many tokens the drafter can get right in a row, and on-policy distillation, the approach aimed at this problem, is tied to sequential draft-verify rollouts while collecting its training signal. SpecOPD starts from the observation that this sequential dependence is not essential to on-policy learning.

item.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

Speculative decoding is a technique that commits multiple tokens together when a large model is invoked once, accelerating language model decoding where memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. This paper points out that public implementations of this technique fail to capture much of the permissible speedup, and has a coding agent re-measure the bottleneck for each deployment environment and discover optimizations on its own. The result is a large increase in speedup for both single requests and batching, without training or loss of output quality.

item.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

As context grows longer, softmax attention’s compute grows quadratically with context length, and the key-value cache grows proportionally to context length. Linear attention, which avoids this, compresses context into a fixed-size matrix memory, but the problem remained that editing that memory disturbs other memories already stored. This paper proposes the Kronecker delta rule, which narrows the scope touched by a single update, and KronLSTM, which implements it as gates.

item.title: TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving
item.description:
Paper

TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving

Original: Shuhuai Li et al., “TAO: Tool-Aware Joint Scheduling for LLM-Based Agentic Serving” (arXiv:2610.37230v1, preprint). The following account is based solely on the attached original text.

Introduction

Agents alternate between model inference and external tool execution. While a tool runs, that session’s GPU demand becomes suspendable; how this gap is used and which node the session is attached to when it returns determine response time. This paper proposes TAO, a framework that binds both problems into a single scheduling problem.

item.title: Look Only When Needed: Certificate-Guided Visual Routing for Efficient Diffusion VLMs
item.description:
Paper

The problem: re-reading the image at every step

Diffusion language models that answer questions from images do not complete a response in one pass. While filling in the blanks over many steps, they re-read an image that barely changes from the beginning at every step. LOWN asks “does this step really need the image?” every time, and re-reads only when necessary, cutting decoding cost substantially.

item.title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
item.description:
Paper

Diffusion language models must decide ‘what’ and ‘where’ at the same time

Diffusion language models generate sentences by repeatedly filling masked tokens. To decode exactly, each model forward must commit only the single most certain masked position as a token, which is slow; committing multiple positions at once to increase speed degrades generation quality. This paper moves speculative decoding, a lossless acceleration technique validated on autoregressive models, to diffusion language models, but finds the solution by predicting not tokens but the order of which position to fill next.

item.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

In settings where the batch size is close to 1, such as conversational services, the latency of a mixture-of-experts language model comes mostly from reading the routed expert weights from GPU memory. Most of the intermediate dimensions inside an expert contribute little to a token, so choosing which channels to read first can substantially reduce the amount read. This paper shows that two objectives that existing channel selectors try to meet through calibration data are in fact not achieved, and presents a selector built from model weights alone, without calibration.

item.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
item.description: Paper Recent language models keep increasing the amount of information packed into a single vocabulary entry. Per-layer embeddings (PLE), first introduced in Gemma 3n, carried over to Gemma 4: instead of a single input-layer vector per vocabulary item, each decoder layer has a different learned vector. This post examines OPTIC, which shrinks this table by about 100× while retaining most of the original performance, starting from the problem setting and proceeding through a small example, the method, results, and limitations.

item.title: Intern Lumina U2: A Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation
item.description:
Paper

Problem: Why It’s Hard to Unify Understanding and Generation in One Representation

There have been many attempts to merge image understanding and image generation into a single model. Most, however, optimize the two abilities separately in different representation spaces. When text is trained as a token classification problem and images are trained with a diffusion/flow objective over continuous vectors, the two objectives push against each other within one backbone, which tends to make training unstable.

item.title: Matrix-Game 4.0: Harnessing Video Models for Real-Time Playable Game Worlds
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

A game world built by a video generation model alone stores off-screen state nowhere. Every time a corridor you have already passed through is redrawn, it changes, and rules such as health have to be read back from pixels. Matrix-Game 4.0 has the game engine enforce rules and state in code, while the video model is responsible only for rendering the screen.

item.title: Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression
item.description:
Paper

Introduction

In models that handle long contexts, the compression operation that reduces multiple tokens to a single vector becomes a performance bottleneck. This paper reframes compression not as a choice of weighted averaging, but as the problem of finding the coefficients of a regression problem defined by the tokens. TTR-Compressor constructs a label-free ridge regression problem from the input tokens and uses its closed-form solution as the compressed representation.

item.title: Large Flow Language Models
item.description:
Paper

The sequential bottleneck of sampling one token at a time

Large language models can compute an entire sentence in parallel during training, but when generating text they must know the preceding token before they can choose the next one. No matter how fast the GPU is, this order cannot be skipped in one pass, so generation latency grows. This post covers Lafa (Large flow language model), which attacks this bottleneck with block-level flow.

item.title: Cache Engineering for Agents
item.description:
Paper

The Cost and Accuracy Dilemma of Long Agent Trajectories

LLM agents accumulate long trajectories by repeating reasoning and tool calls for hundreds of rounds. To make inference fast, the already-computed key-value (KV) cache must stay on the GPU and be read again for each next token; as the trajectory grows, storage and read costs increase. The paper measures KV cache reads at 82.4% of total API cost (§1, Figure 13), and points out that accuracy degrades once the number of KVs or the positional span handled by attention exceeds what the model can handle (§1).

item.title: Speculative Sampling in Interactive Video Generation
item.description:
Paper

Staying Instantly Responsive While Keeping Large Chunks: Speculative Sampling for Interactive Video Generation

When a viewer changes a camera move or an action command, the video being played must change with it right away. But no matter how fast a video generation model is, a new condition only reaches the screen at chunk granularity, and the user waits until that boundary. This paper removes the wait floor imposed by boundaries through speculative sampling that generates at large size while committing the output in small pieces.

item.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
item.description:
Paper

MemT-1.0: A Memory Foundation Model That Puts Conversational Memory Inside Model Computation

For a chatbot or coding agent to process an ongoing conversation with full context, it must feed all text so far into the input at every turn. Attention must hold the key/value of that entire text in a cache, and the cache grows in proportion to the token count as the conversation lengthens. Instead of replaying past conversation as text, MemT-1.0 compresses it into a fixed-size state (a matrix) inside the model, and at question time accesses the past history through that state to answer.

item.title: DLite: History-free Speculative Decoding for Agentic AI
item.description:
As a coding agent reads files and calls tools, its conversation and execution history grows. Adding a small model to draft answers faster can create another burden if that model must separately process and retain the same long history.

DLite lets the target model handle the history, while the small drafter uses the target’s internal representations to propose upcoming tokens. It removes the drafter’s separate historical KV cache. It does not remove the target’s cache or discard historical information.

item.title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention
item.description:
Training on long documents across several GPUs creates more than a compute problem. Each GPU also needs the right attention mask: the rules that determine which tokens may attend to which other tokens. If those rules leave one GPU with more work than the others, the entire training step waits for it.

FlashMask-3 starts with how masks are stored, then uses that representation to select work, distribute it, and overlap communication with computation. The paper reports a 7.3–11.0% improvement in full training throughput for a MoE model with a 128K context on 128 H100 GPUs. That result must be distinguished from the speedup of the attention kernel alone (§4.3, Table 1).

item.title: HLA-WM: Hybrid Linear Attention for Long-Horizon Video World Models
item.description:
Paper

arXiv:2610.05739 · Monash University · The University of Adelaide · Zhejiang University

One-Line Summary (TL;DR)

Recurrent linear attention (Gated DeltaNet) in video world models compresses memory into a fixed-size state, which is efficient, but when the camera leaves and returns, distant scenes are progressively forgotten. HLA-WM caches chunk-level affine summaries in a training-free way and uses camera geometry (frustum overlap) to retrieve and recompose the relevant scenes, achieving PSNR +0.74 dB, rotation error −28.5%, and a 12× reduction versus Full KV in history memory over a 60-second rollout (about 6× the memory of GDN) (source: §Abstract, Fig. 1).

item.title: Contextual Correction of Parallel Drafts for Speculative Decoding
item.description:
Paper

TL;DR — Parallel diffusion drafters like DFlash produce a whole block of tokens at once, but within the block they predict each token without knowing the identity of the preceding tokens. DCOCO is a lightweight corrector that re-selects contextually appropriate tokens by scoring the adjacent transitions among already-drafted candidates in a single batched operation, with no extra drafter forward pass. Across 4 backbones and 10 benchmarks it is up to 6.6× faster than vanilla and up to 18% faster than the strongest speculative baseline, and it retains a 6–23% margin even at concurrency of 4–32 streams.

item.title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part II: Rethinking at Fixed Points
item.description:
Paper

TL;DR

In looped language models, the state converges to a fixed point $z^\star = F_\theta(z^\star; x)$ as the recursion depth grows, and near the fixed point the “endpoint” can stand in for the entire trajectory. This paper uses that one property to reduce four different costs at once across pretraining, serving, and RL: (1) training backpropagates only through the last $b$ recursions (truncated BPTT), (2) decoding caches only the last KV bank for each token (terminal KV sharing, a $3\times$ cut in cache), (3) prefill is distilled into a lightweight student that predicts the fixed point directly, giving up to a $1.79\times$ speedup, and (4) RL reuses gradients from stored rollout states to make updates $2\times$ faster. It also improves the two devices that actually produce this fixed point — the depth prior and input injection — as a “learned prior” and “orthogonal injection (OrthoInj)” respectively, lowering perplexity across the whole range from 100M to 1.6B parameters (source: §1).

item.title: SparseDecoding: Decoding-Aware Pruning for Accurate and Efficient LLM Inference
item.description:
Paper

TL;DR

Observing that LLM autoregressive decoding is memory-bound, this work collects the calibration for pruning not from “fixed text” but from “tokens the model generates itself,” and attaches a decoding-specific (SpMV) $N{:}M$ kernel to it, achieving up to $1.48\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup.

item.title: MC-Sparse: Deconstructing and Closing the Dense-Sparse Attention Gap in Diffusion Transformers
item.description:
Paper

TL;DR

By making the attention of a diffusion transformer (DiT) sparse at the token level without training, while caching and reusing accurate KV selections and dense–sparse output residuals at anchor steps, it achieves up to a $2.32\times$ denoising speedup in video and 3D generation with no quality loss (source: Fig. teaser, §Abstract).

item.title: TokenRouter: Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing
item.description:
Paper

TokenRouter: An Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing

TL;DR — Routing an LLM at the token level rather than the session/query level can substantially push out the cost–quality Pareto frontier, but it has been hard to put into practice on existing serving stacks (vLLM, SGLang) that are tied to a single-LLM assumption, due to step desynchronization, batch admission delay, and implementation complexity. Under the principle of “request-centric programming, model-centric execution,” TokenRouter introduces asynchronous subservers and a delayed batching scheduler, achieving 2.01–64.15× decoding throughput over existing implementations across five routing algorithms and several model pairs (source: §Abstract, §1).

item.title: Mechanics of Long-Context Hybrid Models Part 1.1: From Hybrid Attention to Hybrid Position
item.description:
Paper

Mechanics of Long-Context Hybrid Models: From Hybrid Attention to Hybrid Position

TL;DR — These days open-source LLMs are rapidly shifting from models that “use full attention only” to hybrid models that “mix full attention with Sliding-Window Attention (SWA) or Linear Attention (LA).” This paper mechanistically dissects “why” hybrid models work and “how” they can be designed better. The key conclusion is that the true identity of a hybrid model is in fact not hybrid attention but hybrid position (NoPE + position-biased attention). It identifies a Seesaw Effect — SWA hybrids are strong at length extrapolation but flip on context extension — and a No-Free-Lunch Effect — LA hybrids are strong within the training length but weak at extrapolation. As a solution it proposes Sliding-Window Linear Attention (SWLA), which extrapolates 4k→64k, i.e. 16× without training, while maintaining 100% accuracy on NIAH-SK1.
